column2: Lavalle and the Fall of Dorrego

The Army of the South has come home from the Brazilian war unpaid and unhappy, and on the first of December General Juan Lavalle marched it into the Fort and turned Governor Dorrego out of office. Dorrego has fled into the campana to raise the militia of the countryside, and Colonel Rosas has ridden south to join him. The Unitarian officers want the matter settled at Navarro with a firing squad and no trial. The alternative is to treat with a man the army has already proclaimed a traitor, and to admit that the city cannot govern the province alone.
Shoot him at Navarro. The province needs one law.
Dorrego lives. Come to terms with the Federal militias.
The Army of the South Seizes Buenos Aires

The regiments that fought the Empire of Brazil have overthrown the government they were raised to defend. General Lavalle holds the Fort of Buenos Aires and the deposed Governor Dorrego is in the open country with the militia of the estancias behind him. Whether the quarrel ends in a compact or in a volley, the provinces of the River Plate have learned that the city is held by whoever the cavalry obeys.
General Lavalle has deposed Governor Dorrego and holds the Fort of Buenos Aires. The deposed governor is raising the militia of the campana against the returning army.
Lavalle deposes Dorrego in Buenos Aires.
The Restorer of the Laws

The countryside will not obey the city. Juan Manuel de Rosas commands the militia of the campana, the estancieros pay it, and the Sala de Representantes is being asked to name him governor with the facultades extraordinarias, powers no governor of Buenos Aires has ever held. His partisans call him the Restorer of the Laws. The alternative is a ministry of lawyers and merchants out of the Unitarian salons of the port: learned, respectable, and without a single squadron of horse behind it.
Name Rosas governor with extraordinary powers.
A government of educated men, under the constitution.
Buenos Aires Debates the Extraordinary Powers

The Sala de Representantes of Buenos Aires must choose between the colonel of the rural militia and the doctors of the city. Juan Manuel de Rosas asks for the facultades extraordinarias and promises order in the campana in exchange, while the Unitarian party offers constitutional government and can guarantee nothing outside the walls. Montevideo is already filling with men who expect to lose.
The Sala de Representantes of Buenos Aires weighs extraordinary powers for Juan Manuel de Rosas against a constitutional ministry drawn from the Unitarian party.
Buenos Aires weighs extraordinary powers for Rosas.
The Federal Pact and the League of the Interior

The provinces cannot agree what the nation is. Buenos Aires, Santa Fe, Entre Rios and Corrientes are offered a Federal Pact: a league of sovereign provinces, a joint commission sitting at Santa Fe, a common enemy and no constitution at all until the country is at peace. General Paz answers from Cordoba with a League of the Interior, nine provinces under one military command, a treasury, a mint and a state to be built by force if the littoral will not consent to it.
Sign the Federal Pact. A league, not a state.
Stand with Paz and the League of the Interior.
Two Leagues Divide the River Plate

The Argentine provinces have split into two confederations. The littoral has signed a Federal Pact that binds four provinces without governing any of them, while nine provinces of the interior have accepted the command of General Paz and the promise of a unified state. Both leagues claim to speak for the nation and neither has a congress. Foreign merchants at the port are advised that no treaty signed at Buenos Aires binds Cordoba.
The Argentine provinces have divided between the Federal Pact of the littoral and General Paz and his League of the Interior. Neither confederation has a constitution.
The Argentine provinces split into two leagues.
The Campaign of the Desert

South of the Salado the estancias end and the malon begins. Every summer the mounted bands come north for cattle and captives, and every winter the frontier line stands a little further back than it did. The estancieros have subscribed the money for a campaign to the Rio Negro, three divisions marching abreast to clear the pampa in a single season. The cheaper answer is a chain of forts, ransomed captives and the yearly presents of mares, yerba and tobacco that keep the friendly caciques friendly.
March to the Rio Negro.
A line of forts and treaties with the caciques.
The Argentine Frontier Moves South

Argentine columns have crossed the Salado and pushed the frontier of settlement toward the Rio Negro. The estancieros who paid for the expedition are already surveying the ground they expect to be granted, and the ports of the south are being fortified. For the peoples of the pampa it is the end of a century of raiding on their own terms. For Buenos Aires it is a new province of grass.
Argentine columns have crossed the Salado and carried the frontier of settlement south toward the Rio Negro, opening the pampa to the estancias.
Argentina carries its frontier south to the pampa.
Barranca Yaco

Facundo Quiroga was ambushed and shot dead in his coach at Barranca Yaco on the road out of Cordoba, and the Reinafe brothers are named in every account of it. The one man the interior feared is gone and the provinces are looking to Buenos Aires for a verdict. The Sala offers the governor the suma del poder publico, the whole public power, with no limit of term and no appeal. The other road is a trial for the murderers and a constituent congress that would write the constitution the country has never had.
Grant the governor the whole public power.
Try the murderers and call a constituent congress.
General Quiroga Murdered on the Cordoba Road

Facundo Quiroga, the caudillo of the Argentine interior, was shot dead with his whole party at Barranca Yaco while returning from a mission of mediation. The killing has left Buenos Aires without a rival in the provinces and has been answered by a demand that the governor be given the entire public power of the state. Whether the answer is a dictatorship or a constituent congress will settle the shape of the River Plate for a generation.
The caudillo Facundo Quiroga has been murdered at Barranca Yaco. Buenos Aires must now choose between granting the governor the whole public power and calling a constituent congress.
Quiroga is murdered at Barranca Yaco.
